per_ply.system_comment: The game opens as a King's Pawn Game (B00).

per_ply.human_comment:
Of course the most popular opening of the
mid-19th century. Conventional wisdom at the time assumed that White had an
obligation to fight for the initiative at any price. That is why material
sacrifice at an early stage of the game was simply a show of good taste, and
to decline the opponent's kind material offer was not considered an honourable
option.

per_ply.system_comment: Black sacrifices material with 9...c6!!, maintaining the advantage (-1.36, Stockfish:16) after [pv:c6 dxc6 Nxc6 Nxc6 bxc6]. The move immediately targets the bishop on b5, keeping Black clearly better even at the cost of a line where White may win a rook and see its pawn structure improved. By contrast, 9...Kf8 leads to only a slight advantage for Black [pv:Kf8 O-O Qxh4 Bxf4 Bxe5], with White's king set to come under pressure deeper in the line—a slower payoff than the direct sacrificial plan.

The most accurate move is 10.dxc6, which gives Black a winning advantage (-1.58, Stockfish:16); the line runs [pv:dxc6 Nxc6 Nxc6 bxc6 Bxc6+]. At the cost of play that may leave Black with a strong knight on g3—a centralized outpost that can cramp White's coordination. A comparable option was 10.Bc4, which also gives Black a winning advantage along [pv:Bc4 b5 Bb3 O-O O-O], where Black's pawn structure could weaken in the line while White's rooks may become active on the open files.

White missed the potential to preserve a bishop for a knight and reduce Black to a single bishop, weakening the bishop-pair edge that often counts in open middlegames, with 11.Bc4, which leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Bc4 O-O O-O Bxe5 dxe5]. Playing 11.Nxc6 instead makes matters worse, and Black now holds a winning advantage (-1.22 → -1.72, Stockfish:16) [pv:Nxc6 Nxc6 Bxc6+ Kf8 Bxa8].

Black's 11...Nxc6!! is a sacrifice that maintains the advantage (-1.55, Stockfish:16), and the main line [pv:Nxc6 Bxc6+ Kf8 Bxa8 Ng3] shows how...Kf8 meets the check before Bxa8 may set up...Ng3 to increase pressure on White's king. Giving up material for lasting initiative often works when the remaining pieces stay active. A comparable option was 11...Qb6, which also leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Qb6 Nxa7+ Bd7 Qxg4 Rxa7] by immediately targeting the bishop on b5.

White's 13.Bxa8 gives Black a winning advantage (-1.58, Stockfish:16), and the main line continues [pv:Bxa8 Ng3 Rh2 Kg7 Kf2]. A comparable option was 13.Qd3, which also gives Black a winning advantage [pv:Qd3 Ng3 Rf1 Nxf1 Qxf1] but would have kept White's pieces actively placed—active pieces find useful squares and create counterplay more easily.

Ng3 is the most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-1.60, Stockfish:16): it leaves White with a hanging piece, improves Black's piece activity, and targets the rook on h1, while the line may set Black's rooks to grow more active on the open files [pv:Ng3 Rh2 Kg7 Kf2 Re8]. Active pieces sustain counterplay even though White is up a rook; Kg7 is a comparable option that also gives Black a winning advantage [pv:Kg7 Nc3 Ng3 Kf2 Nxh1+].

per_ply.system_comment: This pawn advance is a losing blunder: 20.a4 leads to forced mate for Black (#4 for Black, Stockfish:16) [pv:a4], surrendering all resistance in a sharp middlegame where one slip ends the game. White missed the chance to win a piece and leave Black with a hanging piece via 20.Rh3, which leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Rh3 gxh3 dxe5 Qb6+ Kf3] — a materially better path that at least grabs material before Black's forcing kingside checks take over.

Black plays the strongest continuation with Qf1+, a forcing check that leads to forced mate (#3 for Black, Stockfish:16) [pv:Qf1+]. White has no satisfactory defense and cannot sidestep the line; after the queens come off on f1, Black's kingside checks keep the white king under fire, tie down defenders, and the attack delivers forced mate.

White's 21.Qxf1 leads to forced mate for Black (#3 for Black, Stockfish:16) [pv:Qxf1]. The queen trade on f1 offers White no compensation; Black's...Bxd4+ may add another forcing check to the kingside attack, keeping the king under fire and tying down defenders until...Re1# finishes the line. With nothing gained from the exchange, White only hastens a mating sequence that cannot be parried.

With Bxd4+, Black adds a forcing check to the kingside attack, keeping White's king under fire and tying down defenders. This move leads to forced mate for Black (#2 for Black, Stockfish:16) [pv:Bxd4+]. Bringing more force to bear on the king is how such attacks turn decisive, and White's attempts to block the assault may only hasten a mating net.

White's 22.Be3 leads to forced mate for Black (#2 for Black, Stockfish:16) [pv:Be3]. The bishop move provides no defensive answer, and Black's kingside attack is set to conclude on the next move with...Re1#, delivering mate with no legal reply for White. After this slip, White's only choices lead down the same road to a forced checkmate within two moves.
